title: Three of us bought a house we can barely afford. Should we refinance or sell our apartment?
excerpt: Three single brothers bought a RM1 million terrace house and have nothing left to renovate it. Sean calls the purchase a mistake and compares refinancing their Klang apartment with selling it.

question.asker: From S, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: S, 43, and his brothers, 45 and 37, are single and earn about RM12,000 a month between them. In 2013 S and his younger brother bought a Klang apartment from the developer for RM265,000; about RM180,000 of the loan is left, similar units are listed at about RM320,000 to RM380,000, and it would rent for about RM1,000 to RM1,300 furnished. Last year all three bought a double-storey terrace house in Shah Alam from the developer for about RM1.04 million with an 85% loan over 30 years, so all live together. Keys are due at the end of 2024, when the RM4,300 instalment starts, and they have no money left for renovation.
question.text: Should they refinance or sell the Klang apartment to pay for renovation, and was the house a risky buy?

answer.quote: Buying the property was a very, very big mistake.
answer.summary: Yes, the house was a mistake: it needs three incomes to service and they paid above subsale prices. Now they can either refinance the apartment, freeing about RM124,000 while the rent roughly covers the new instalment, or sell it for about RM200,000 after the loan and rent somewhere until the keys come. Sean would refinance and keep it, if they can handle a vacant month.

reasons.title: New homes are priced ahead
reasons.body: Developers price in future growth: similar subsale terraces nearby sell for about RM850,000 to RM900,000, so they paid about RM100,000 more and shouldn't expect quick gains. A sale soon wouldn't clear the loan comfortably either.

reasons.title: Refinancing frees cash but raises the instalment
reasons.body: At a RM380,000 valuation, an 80% loan of about RM304,000 clears the RM180,000 owed and leaves about RM124,000. The new instalment of roughly RM1,200 to RM1,300 is close to the rent, but an empty month comes out of their pockets.

reasons.title: Selling takes months
reasons.body: A sale takes about six months to complete for freehold and about nine for leasehold, so they'd need to time it and rent a place in between. Refinancing and then selling within three months isn't realistic, because the paperwork alone takes that long.

reasons.title: Shared ownership carries extra risk
reasons.body: If one brother loses his job, marries or wants his share out, the others must cover or buy him out. A rise in interest rates would also push the RM4,300 instalment higher.

actions: Ask your bank's mortgage department for a valuation from its panel valuers, and compare it with listings on property portals.
Decide on a basic renovation budget first; for a bare terrace house, Sean estimates about RM70,000 to RM80,000 for essentials.
If you refinance, keep the extra cash as a buffer for months when the apartment is empty.
If you sell, park what's left after renovating in a flexi or semi-flexi loan account to cut interest.
Agree in writing how the brothers will share costs, and what happens if one wants to leave.
caveat: Sean's preferred option suits brothers who can tolerate the apartment sitting empty for a while; if they can't, selling is the safer choice. With hindsight, he would have rented a large house and let out the apartment instead of buying.
sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #225. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in October 2023, and the refinancing sums are Sean's rough examples.
